title: Rhetorical technique Practice 1
description: 4 short texts - 8 focused rhetorical technique questions
subject: rla
passage:
TEXT A - Tree Letter

"Shade where we walk. Shade where we wait. Shade where children play," repeats a neighborhood letter calling for more street trees.

TEXT B - Clinic Story

A report about appointment reminders opens with one patient describing how a missed voicemail led to a missed specialist visit.

TEXT C - Water Number

A conservation page notes that repairing one leaking toilet can save thousands of liters of water over a year.

TEXT D - Park Question

"If the path is unusable after every heavy rain, can we really call it an all-weather route?" asks an advocacy group.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: The repeated opening "Shade where..." uses parallel wording to emphasize the range of places that need shade.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: rhetorical question
options.whyWrong: The lines make repeated statements; they do not ask a question.

options.text: statistic
options.whyWrong: No numerical evidence appears.

options.text: anecdote
options.whyWrong: The letter does not tell a personal story.

options.text: repetition with parallel phrasing

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: Repetition and parallel structure turn separate locations into one accumulating call for shade.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It proves with measured data that every listed location is dangerously hot.
options.whyWrong: The technique creates emphasis; it does not supply measurements.

options.text: It defines the technical meaning of urban shade for the reader.
options.whyWrong: The repeated phrases do not function as a definition.

options.text: It softens the request by making the need for trees sound uncertain.
options.whyWrong: The repetition strengthens emphasis rather than weakening it.

options.text: The repeated opening builds emphasis and makes several everyday public spaces feel connected to the same need.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: The report opens with one patient's experience to make the communication problem concrete.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: anecdote
statistic
options.whyWrong: The example describes one person rather than numerical data.

options.text: analogy
options.whyWrong: The report does not explain the problem by comparing it with a different familiar situation.

options.text: rhetorical question
options.whyWrong: No question is posed.

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: An anecdote can help readers see how an abstract communication failure affects a real person without proving how common it is.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: The personal example makes the communication problem concrete before the report presents broader evidence.
It establishes by itself that missed voicemails are the main cause of missed visits for all patients.
options.whyWrong: One patient's experience cannot establish prevalence or the main cause for everyone.

options.text: It defines the clinic's reminder policy in formal terms.
options.whyWrong: The story illustrates a problem rather than defining policy.

options.text: It compares two reminder systems using the same criteria.
options.whyWrong: The anecdote presents one experience, not a structured comparison.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: The number of liters gives a measurable estimate of the scale of possible water savings.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: anecdote
options.whyWrong: No individual person's story is told.

options.text: statistic / quantified example
analogy
options.whyWrong: The statement does not compare leak repair with another situation.

options.text: rhetorical question
options.whyWrong: The sentence states a quantity rather than asking a question.

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: A numerical estimate gives readers a sense of scale, though the number still needs relevant context to support a broader claim.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It proves that every leaking toilet wastes exactly the same amount of water.
options.whyWrong: A quantified example does not establish identical results in every case.

options.text: It creates urgency mainly through emotional language about waste.
options.whyWrong: The force comes from a quantity, not emotionally loaded wording.

options.text: The quantity makes the potential water savings concrete and easier to evaluate.
It explains the mechanical steps required to repair a toilet.
options.whyWrong: The statistic measures potential savings rather than giving instructions.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: The advocacy group asks a question whose wording challenges whether the repeatedly flooded path deserves the label "all-weather."
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: statistic
options.whyWrong: No numerical data is given.

options.text: anecdote
options.whyWrong: The sentence does not tell a personal story.

options.text: rhetorical question
analogy
options.whyWrong: No comparison to a different situation is used.

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: The rhetorical question invites readers to reconsider the label rather than simply requesting information.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It neutrally asks officials to provide the date of the next flood.
options.whyWrong: The question is persuasive, not a request for factual information.

options.text: The question challenges the claim that the route works in all weather by directing attention to repeated flooding.
It proves that the path is unusable after every kind of rainfall.
options.whyWrong: The wording refers to heavy rain and repeated flooding, not every rainfall condition.

options.text: It defines the engineering standard for an all-weather route.
options.whyWrong: The question challenges a label but does not provide a technical definition.
